title: Pennsylvania Lifers Fight to Break Legislative Stalemate, and Find a Pathway Out of Prison
author: Victoria Law
content:
In March, the more than 1,000 people sentenced to life without parole for
felony murder convictions in Pennsylvania finally had hope that they might not
die in prison after all.  

That’s when the Pennsylvania Supreme Court
[ruled](https://boltsmag.org/pennsylvania-supreme-court-life-without-parole-
felony-murder/) that the state’s especially harsh practice of automatically
sentencing people to life without parole for felony murder—a charge allowing
prosecutions for murder due to someone’s involvement in a crime that led to a
death, even if they didn’t personally cause or participate in the
killing—violated the state constitution’s protections against “cruel
punishments.” Pennsylvania was one of just two states to mandate that anyone
convicted of felony murder, which is classified as second-degree murder in the
state, receive a sentence of life without parole.

While the ruling only changed things for a single person at that moment—Derek
Lee, who was sentenced to life without parole more than a decade ago for his
participation in a 2014 burglary in which his accomplice fatally shot the
homeowner during a struggle—it looked like the court’s decision in his case
could pave a pathway out of prison for more than 1,000 Pennsylvanians serving
a mandatory life without parole sentence for felony murder. Even though the
court declined to make its decision retroactive, it gave the legislature a 120
day deadline to “consider appropriate remedial measures.”

But those four months passed without lawmakers agreeing on how to respond to
the court’s order. The state’s Republican-controlled Senate passed a
[bill](https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/sb1400) imposing a
minimum of 35 years in prison before people who were already convicted of
felony murder could apply for parole. The Senate bill also created a mandatory
minimum sentence of 35 years for anyone convicted of felony murder in the
future, with some exceptions for defendants who meet mitigating circumstances.
And it still preserved the option for judges to choose a sentence of life
without parole for felony murder under certain aggravating circumstances.

The House, under Democratic control, thought the Senate’s legislation was [too
harsh](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/07/pennsylvania-felony-murder-
deadline-state-legislature-justice-system/) and passed a bill that didn’t
specify a mandatory minimum for felony murder. The House
[bill](https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb1042) also established
that the hundreds of people already convicted of felony murder should be
considered for parole after a minimum of 30 years in prison. Ultimately, the
two chambers [never agreed on a
compromise](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/07/pennsylvania-felony-
murder-missed-deadline-justice-system/).

But there’s a possibility for change in the near future. Democrats gained full
control of Pennsylvania’s state government on Nov. 3, which gives them the
power to set policies in the state, a first since the early 1990s.

They flipped the state Senate and expanded their majority in the state House.
Governor Josh Shapiro, who had filed an amicus brief in support of Lee’s
appeal and then applauded the supreme court’s decision this spring, easily won
a second term over a Republican who [faulted](https://www.mcrwpa.org/garrity-
demands-action-for-crime-victims-and-the-preservation-of-public-safety)
[Democrats](https://whyy.org/articles/pennsylvania-election-2026-governor-
debate-shapiro-garrity/) for making it too easy for people convicted of
second-degree murder to be released.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/PA-Justices.jpg)Justice
Debra Todd, left, wrote the majority opinion in the March ruling that struck
down life without parole as an automatic punishment for felony murder. Here
she stands with Justice Kevin Dougherty, a fellow Democrat who joined that
ruling. (Photo from PA Courts/Facebook)

Sean Damon with [Straight Ahead](https://straight-ahead.org/our-legislative-
agenda/), an organization dedicated to ending life without parole throughout
Pennsylvania, says that the new Democratic trifecta could make criminal legal
reforms more likely to pass next year.

“It’s a more hopeful landscape,” he told _Bolts_ , adding that lawmakers
across the spectrum already seem to agree that people convicted of felony
murder should get a chance to someday rejoin their communities. “The Senate
Republicans, Dave Sunday (the Republican Attorney General), Governor Shapiro,
the House Democrats, everybody agrees,” he told _Bolts_. “The question is how
much time and what the new sentence should be.”

People who have already spent decades behind bars aren’t waiting for
legislative action, however, and have been asking the supreme court to take
matters into its own hands. A week after the ruling in Lee’s case this past
spring, Jerome Coffey filed a petition challenging the felony murder
conviction that’s kept him in prison for more than three decades. And in late
September, the state supreme court announced that it was willing to take up
Coffey’s [argument](https://abolitionistlawcenter.org/2026/09/29/pa-supreme-
court-to-address-retroactivity-for-unconstitutional-second-degree-murder-
sentences/) that the ruling should apply to his case retroactively. What the
court decides could determine resentencing proceedings for Coffey and others.

“While the Pennsylvania legislature has failed to address retroactivity,
despite bipartisan support for this general idea, we look to the Pennsylvania
Supreme Court to ensure that its decision in _Lee_ is fairly applied to more
than a thousand people serving a life sentence for felony murder,” Rupalee
Rashatwar, managing attorney of the Abolitionist Law Center, which is
representing Coffey, told _Bolts._ She called the court’s decision to consider
Coffey’s case “the culmination of decades of organizing against death by
incarceration sentences.”

“His case shows us the collective power we can build when movements come
together to hope for a better world,” Rashatwar said, “a world where those who
never intended to take a life have a right to be judged individually and for
their own actions, a world with a glimmer of hope after 33 years of
incarceration.”

* * *

Coffey’s attorneys say that a litany of problems with his felony murder
conviction, which he has spent 33 years fighting, exemplify the urgent need
for the state supreme court to enforce its ruling this past March and apply it
retroactively to him and others.

Philadelphia prosecutors accused Coffey of being involved in a 1992 murder,
alleging that he helped abduct and move the victim before a co-conspirator
shot and killed him. At trial, they presented no physical evidence, resting
their case solely on shaky eyewitness testimony.

One key witness in the case, Nemo Kennedy, recanted his initial statement to
police that implicated Coffey before he went to trial. Kennedy then claimed
during a pretrial hearing that he and a family member had been threatened by
police, and that he had feared being charged as the shooter if he didn’t name
Coffey.

Still, prosecutors put Kennedy on the stand during the 1994 joint trial for
Coffey and his co-defendant. Kennedy was vague in his testimony, simply saying
that on the night of the shooting, Coffey came to his house and told him he
“just did something.” He also testified that two days later during a phone
call, he told Coffey that people were saying that he’d killed Moss, to which
Coffey allegedly responded that he “don’t care what people say.”

Kennedy also admitted during his testimony that he had been consuming PCP,
codeine, and marijuana coated in embalming fluid both on the night of the
killing and when he was first questioned by police.

One jailhouse informant testified that Coffey’s alleged co-conspirator
confessed to the shooting and that Coffey threatened the informant’s sister if
she testified against them at their trial. But a jail official demonstrated
during testimony that the two men were never in the same housing unit and
would never have had a chance to interact.

Coffey’s court-appointed defense attorney offered up his mother and twin
sister as alibi witnesses. Both testified that Coffey was at home with them on
the night of the shooting, which was the same day that his sister returned
from the hospital with her newborn baby. Rashatwar, the Abolitionist Law
Center attorney currently helping represent Coffey in his appeals, says that
30 years after the trial, her team uncovered that the prosecution had records
confirming that his sister was discharged from the hospital the day of the
shooting, but never gave those records to Coffey’s trial lawyer and didn’t
present them at trial. So the jury never got to see those records that seemed
to confirm their alibi testimony.

Coffey was convicted of second-degree murder and given a mandatory sentence of
life without the possibility of parole. His co-defendant, Lee Smith, was
acquitted.

In the decades following his 1994 trial, lawyer after lawyer abandoned Coffey
as he tried to appeal his conviction—a common experience for Pennsylvanians
trying to appeal their convictions due to lax rules, paltry pay, and crushing
caseloads for court-appointed lawyers in the state, [as ProPublica recently
reported](https://www.propublica.org/article/post-conviction-legal-system-
finley-judges-pennsylvania?utm_source=TMP-
Newsletter&utm_campaign=79559ba076-EMAIL_CAMPAIGN_2026_11_10_11_38&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_5e02cdad9d-79559ba076-174315857).

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/IMG_4689.jpg)Jerome Coffey
has been fighting his conviction and life sentence for more than three
decades. (Photo courtesy of Jeanne Coffey)

Coffey’s first attempt to appeal was dismissed because the court-appointed
lawyer who represented him at trial failed to file a brief. Following the
court reinstating Coffey’s right to appeal, his next lawyer was dismissed from
his case after ghosting him for seven years. The lawyer who took over next
also failed to file a brief and Coffey’s appeal was again dismissed. One of
the other lawyers who was appointed to but hardly touched Coffey’s case was
later imprisoned and disbarred for serving as consigliere for a Baltimore drug
trafficking and money laundering ring.

Things started to change in 2017. By then, Coffey was in solitary confinement
and had been [organizing to improve prison
conditions](https://www.hrcoalition.org/team-board-of-directors). ****The men
in isolation looked out for one another and, if they thought someone was
innocent, would pass their names along to their attorneys. That was how
Coffey’s case eventually came to the attention of the Abolitionist Law Center,
which in 2021 joined his attempts to appeal for his freedom.

This past March, Coffey’s lawyers filed his appeal with the state supreme
court a week before it issued the decision in Lee’s case that ruled it
unconstitutional to automatically sentence people with felony murder
convictions to life without parole; Coffey’s lawyers then quickly amended
their petition to add that decision to its list of arguments. While the
supreme court rejected their other claims—such as ineffective assistance of
counsel and the prosecution’s failure to hand over several pieces of
exonerating evidence—it decided to hear Coffey’s argument that the recent
state supreme court ruling should allow him the possibility of resentencing.

Coffey’s twin sister Jeanne is hoping that further action from the courts or
legislature could give her brother a chance at freedom. She still calls him
“Hoagie” because he had a penchant for eating the sandwiches before the start
of his legal nightmare. She recalled how the 2017 election of Larry Krasner as
Philadelphia District Attorney gave the family hope that his case might get a
fresh look from the prosecutor’s office. Krasner set up a conviction integrity
unit in 2018 to [review](https://www.inquirer.com/news/larry-krasner-
conviction-integrity-unit-philadelphia-district-attorney-judges-20190129.html)
possible wrongful convictions, and the unit [produced many
exonerations](https://www.inquirer.com/news/philadelphia-conviction-integrity-
unit-da-larry-krasner-patricia-cummings-20210615.html) in the following years.

Jeanne says their elderly mother, who’d had a stroke by that point, was
especially excited by the idea that her brother had a renewed chance at
someday getting out. “The only thing she really wanted was to see her son
coming home,” Jeanne recalled.

But Krasner’s office ultimately declined to review his case. Later, his office
opposed his post-conviction relief act petition and the court agreed that,
despite the many irregularities, these were not prejudicial and there was not
a reasonable probability of a different trial outcome.

“There were so many things that were wrong in this case, and if you combine
all of them together, that would have led to a different outcome,” Rashatwar
with the Abolitionist Law Center said about Coffey’s case. “If you try to
whittle it down to just one thing, you're missing the bigger picture of all
these problems that happened in this trial.”

Coffey’s mother died in October of 2021.

Jeanne says she’s not giving up hope that her brother could come home. She
recalled how during Sunday dinners with their mother, her twin brother used to
pluck food off her plate, joking, “You don’t want that.” Sometimes, he’d swipe
an entire cheeseburger, telling her, “You was having it sit there too long.”

She wants to recreate that feast with him someday. “I want to make him every
type of food just to see what he likes to eat.”

* * *

Among the many Pennsylvanians currently serving life without parole sentences
for felony murder and hoping for a chance at freedom is John Marshall Payne,
who is 71 and has spent more than 40 years in prison.

Much like Coffey, Payne’s 1986 conviction for being involved in a murder
rested not on any physical evidence but rather eyewitness testimony that
raises serious questions. Two of the three key witnesses were incarcerated at
the time and, in exchange for reduced sentences, testified at Payne’s trial
that he’d made statements that implicated him in the murder. One of them was
facing first-degree murder in an unrelated case, for which the prosecutor had
stated he would seek the death penalty; he was allowed to plead down to lesser
charges that allowed him to be released on parole in 2017. The third witness
testified that Payne admitted to being in a house where a woman had been
killed, but upon cross examination, the witness admitted that she wasn’t sure
if Payne had made the alleged statement at all, and that her heavy use of LSD
caused her to “misperceive things.”

Payne’s attorney introduced testimony from multiple other people who
contradicted the testimony of the prosecution’s key witnesses. This included
testimony from his alleged accomplice who stated that he had never even met
Payne; a man who was housed with one of the jailhouse informants, who
testified that the informant told him that he’d learned about details in the
case from a police officer, not from Payne; and a law librarian who testified
that, on the day of Payne’s alleged confession to the second jailhouse
informant, he was working in the law library with him and that the confession
never happened. Nonetheless, the jury convicted Payne of felony murder. He was
sentenced to life without parole.

Payne says he was devastated when he heard his sentence. Both of his daughters
were young at the time, one of them 11 and the other just 18 months old. Like
Coffey, Payne has never accepted the possibility of dying in prison and has
spent his decades in prison trying to challenge his conviction and sentence
any way he could—through court appeals, DNA testing, and a petition for
commutation.

Then came the decision in Lee’s case this past March declaring life without
parole sentences like theirs to be unconstitutional. Payne says he’d been
following Lee’s case, but had tried not to get his hopes up. “It seemed like
everybody expected it, but the courts can be very disappointing,” he said.
“You think you're going to win and you’re going to go home soon, and these
things don't always happen. I wasn't going to set my goals too much on this
case. When it happened, it was just overwhelming.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Payne2.jpg)John Marshall
Payne, right, has spent more than 40 years in prison for his felony murder
conviction. (Photo courtesy of PA Innocence Project)

In September, after the legislature failed to meet the supreme court’s
deadline to pass a bill, Payne and his attorneys at the Pennsylvania Innocence
Project filed what’s called a [King’s Bench
petition](https://www.pacourts.us/Storage/media/pdfs/20210224/033123-extraordinaryjurisdiction-001741.pdf),
which, if granted, allows the state supreme court to decide on issues of
immediate and significant concern, such as whether to apply a precedent-
setting ruling retroactively. Payne and several others sentenced to life
without parole for felony murder also recently signed onto an amicus brief
filed in support of Coffey’s petition that’s now before the state supreme
court.

Payne remembers his last Halloween with his daughters; his older daughter
dressed as a cat, while his baby daughter was too young to really participate
in the festivities. Since then, Payne has missed 40 years of holidays,
birthdays, graduations, weddings, and the births and baptisms of every one of
his five grandchildren.

Both of Payne’s daughters now live outside of Pennsylvania. He says his older
daughter, who recently turned 50, visits four to five times a year, a
considerable expense when factoring in airfare, hotel and the rental car
needed to reach State Correctional Institute Huntington, which is nearly 150
miles from the Pittsburgh airport. Once a year, she brings her three children,
the oldest of whom is now ten, right around the age she was when Payne was
arrested.

Payne now says he’s holding out hope that the case before the state supreme
court or action from lawmakers will soon give him a chance to forge more
memories with his grandchildren, like outings to the park or trips to get ice
cream. “I’m looking forward to that adventure,” he said when reflecting on the
chance to be a grandfather outside the confines of prison.

Terri Harper has also closely followed the state supreme court cases over
Pennsylvania’s especially harsh punishment for felony murder. Harper, who was
also convicted of felony murder and has spent nearly 35 years in prison, says
she believes that Coffey’s appeal that’s currently before the high court “will
be paramount to us getting retroactive relief.” She has less confidence in
lawmakers taking action, even with the recent shakeup in state government,
given their failure to pass reforms this year.

“I don't know if they will stand and make real decisions that affect me and
1,000 others, but I pray all this delay/nothingness will get me to my family,
a new life and my desire to be a voice for a large community of voiceless
human beings,” Harper said in an electronic message to _Bolts_.

Others serving extremely lengthy sentences are closely watching what happens,
in hopes that the tide is turning against such severe sentencing.

Louisa Reyes was 16 years old when she was convicted of second-degree murder
in 2020. Eight years earlier, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that [mandatory
life without parole for people under 18 was
unconstitutional](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/567/460/).
Reyes, who had been 14 when her then-boyfriend killed a friend of her
mother’s, was sentenced to a range of 40 years-to-life instead of life without
parole.

“I'm blessed to have a number in my sentence, but what does 40 years mean?”
Reyes, now 22, reflected in an electronic message to _Bolts_. “My mother is in
her 50s. My father is in his 70s. Will they be alive when I step out into the
world?”

Reyes will be eligible for parole in her 50s. Another bill the Pennsylvania
House considered but didn’t pass this session included a provision allowing
those who were under 15 at the time of the offense to be resentenced between
20 to 30 years. If such a reform passed, Reyes could rejoin her family
sometime between her mid-30s and mid-40s.

“As a child, my sentence made me barren, it took any chance of me building a
love and memory rich life with my sisters and brother, and time that I would
need to build whatever career of my choice,” she reflected.

“In no way am I taking away from the tragedy I was part of upon a family, and
that memory and emotions that come with that night, no matter what sentence I
receive, will be a life sentence of its own,” Reyes continued. “But there
needs to be healing, for both ends. For my mom, who keeps my sandals at the
door as if I were going to walk in any moment from school; for my sisters who
were bullied at school and were rejected from their town because of my
actions; and for my uncle who was harassed to the point where he left
Pennsylvania, never to be seen or heard of again. With a second chance, hope
and healing can return to my family as well as myself.”
